extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (especially those writing queer romance), authors and storytellers seeking guidance on portraying LGBT+ characters
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for crafting queer romance fiction, covering definition, character creation, relationship chemistry, conflict, terminology, and responsible representation of LGBT+ identities and relationship structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a queer romance
rubrics_metrics.description: A queer romance is a love story that involves characters who are LGBT+ (transgender, bisexual, asexual, nonbinary, etc.) and can also include stories that break societal conventions of traditional romance (polyamory, queerplatonic relationships, open relationships).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even relationships that look like a man-woman pairing can be 'queer' if one or both partners are LGBT+. Consider nontraditional relationship structures as queer romance when at least one person involved is under the LGBT+ umbrella.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-discovery as a central plot element
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-discovery often plays a much larger role in queer romances than in heteronormative counterparts; characters frequently must understand their sexuality or gender identity before or during the romance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-discovery can occur at any point—before the story, at first sight, or throughout. One character may be secure while another is in crisis. Ongoing questioning of sexuality after a relationship begins can create internal conflict for the questioning character and emotional conflict for their partner; use this intentionally as character-driven drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: External conflict is common
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict in queer romances often comes from outside the relationship (family disapproval, societal or political pressures) rather than primarily from internal couple differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While queer romances can and do include internal couple conflict, be aware that outside forces (homophobia, legislation, community attitudes) are typical sources of tension; choose the kind of conflict that best serves your story and characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must be interesting, complex, and unique
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are the foundation of a good romance—if characters are not written well as individuals, readers will not care about the romance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write queer characters like any other: give them hobbies, talents, flaws, desires, and histories that extend beyond their sexuality or gender. Use full characterization to make readers invest in both the individual and the relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know terminology and use gender-neutral language appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: If you’re not familiar with LGBT+ terminology, research to ensure you can discuss queer people and lifestyles convincingly; this includes using gender-neutral language when appropriate for characters who use neutral pronouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do research on terms and pronouns; consult resources on nonbinary characters and gender-neutral phrasing. Avoid making mistakes with labels and pronouns—this undermines credibility and may alienate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on tired stereotypes (e.g., all gay men are sassy/flamboyant; all butch lesbians prefer certain types of women; all nonbinary people look androgynous; all trans people get surgery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat each queer character as an individual. Recognize and actively avoid cliché portrayals that reduce characters to caricatures; diversify personalities, occupations, interests, and appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't make queerness the character's entire personality
rubrics_metrics.description: A character's sexuality or gender identity should not be their sole defining trait.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give queer characters separate arcs, hobbies, friendships, ambitions, and flaws that are unrelated to being queer. Show them engaging in everyday activities (rock climbing, painting) without it always relating to their sexuality or gender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not trivialize sexuality, gender, or relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Queer relationships are not less meaningful or legitimate than traditional relationships and should not be portrayed as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with framing and language so the relationship reads as authentic and emotionally valid. Avoid jokes, dismissive portrayals, or plot choices that undermine the legitimacy of the relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid narrow representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid presenting a single queer character or portrayal as representative of an entire community; a single depiction can create a narrow, misleading perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include more than one queer character where possible, or show a broader queer community, to demonstrate diversity of experience. For example, if your only trans character is a party animal, readers may generalize that trait to all trans people; multiple varied depictions prevent that.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tokenization
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use queer characters as tokens—main characters should not be the sole queer person in the entire story merely to 'represent' the group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a diverse range of queer characters and relationships (friends, family, colleagues) so queer characters feel embedded in a believable social world rather than serving solely as representation props.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish relationship compatibility and chemistry convincingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers must be convinced the characters are good for each other; compatibility is about meeting each other's relationship needs, not just opposites or similarities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show what each character finds attractive and what they need in a partner. Establish these traits before the characters fall in love (implicitly or explicitly) so attraction feels natural. Use scenes showing behaviors (e.g., one is disorganized, the other organized and patient) to create believable sparks—show, don't tell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tropes like enemies-to-lovers carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Enemies-to-lovers can work well in queer romance if their initial hatred stems from misunderstanding or bias and aligns with characters' growth arcs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using this trope, make the initial dislike believable (e.g., grounded in internalized bias or misunderstanding) and ensure the characters eventually demonstrate genuine compatibility; avoid contrived hatred that makes reconciliation implausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance depiction of struggle and the right to happy endings
rubrics_metrics.description: Although queer people often face real-world danger and trauma, it's valid and important to write queer romances that are escapist, joyful, and end happily rather than always depicting tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether your story will reflect realistic hardship or provide uplifting representation; both are acceptable. Be mindful of perpetuating only stories of pain—queer people deserve happy, optimistic narratives as well as stories that explore hardship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious using the word 'queer' if you are not part of the community
rubrics_metrics.description: Some individuals may not appreciate writers using the word 'queer' if they are not part of the community because of its history as a reclaimed slur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of discourse around 'queer' and consider audience and character context before using the term; when in doubt, research or consult members of the community.
